## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read

- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). ## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If

  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or

                                       Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


 1   Abstract

 2   Background:

 3   Medical malpractice represents a significant economic cost in healthcare. Increasingly large

 4   damage claims by professional athletes against physicians have raised concerns about the

 5   medicolegal challenges in caring for high-level athletes.

 6   Methods:

 7
                                                                      of
     An online proprietary legal research database was queried for lawsuits related to malpractice in

 8
                                                               ro
     the care of professional and amateur athletes from 1992-2023. Demographics of plaintiffs and

 9
                                                        -p
     defendants, details of lawsuit filings and damages claimed were recorded for all cases,

10
                                                 re
     settlements, and jury verdicts. Descriptive statistics, linear regression, as well as univariate

11                                      lP
     analysis of demographic factors and damage claims in inflation-adjusted 2023 dollars was

12   performed.
                                na
13   Results:                ur
14                Jo
     Eighty-eight lawsuits were recorded from 1992-2023. The sum of indemnities exceeded 186

15   million in 2023 inflation-adjusted United States Dollars. Football players were the most

16   commonly represented athletes (n=26) and represented 49% of total financial awards. Fourteen

17   cases (16%) involved treatment of the upper extremity. Professional and collegiate level of play

18   was associated with higher damages in favor of plaintiffs when compared to other levels of play.

19   No other demographic was associated with higher financial awards. Linear regression showed a

20   significant positive trend with an increasing inflation-adjusted compensation for plaintiff verdicts

21   in the last 30 years.
                                       Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


22   Conclusions:

23   There is an increasing medicolegal financial risk associated with the care of athletes. This is

24   higher in collegiate and professional levels of play. As physicians, insurers and institutions adjust

25   to these financial risks, care must be taken to avoid ramifications on the availability and quality

26   of care provided to athletes. Shoulder and elbow surgeons may consider additional preoperative

27   counseling, legal waiver forms regarding malpractice claims and advocacy for medical

28                                                                    of
     malpractice reforms in the care of athletes with high earning potential to mitigate these

29   increasing financial risks.
                                                               ro
     Level of Evidence: Level IV; Descriptive Epidemiology Study
30
                                                        -p
31                                               re
            Malpractice litigation presents a high economic burden on the United States healthcare

32

33
                                        lP
     system. There is an estimated 4 billion dollars annually in direct cost associated with malpractice

     indemnities and settlements,17 and an estimated 60 billion dollar annual cost to the healthcare

34                                 na
     system as practitioners perform “defensive” medical care.3, 16, 18, 20 These costs stress financially

35                       ur
     challenged hospitals and health systems across the United States.2

36

37
                 Jo
            Surgeons and physicians caring for the athlete face unique challenges related to the

     higher expectations and functional demands of this patient population, and the numerous

38   responsibilities of a team physician.3 Shoulder and elbow surgeons face particularly high

39   medicolegal risk with 15% of orthopedic surgeons facing a lawsuit every year.3, 7, 9, 16, 17 An

40   analysis of 26 years of publicly available orthopedic malpractice lawsuits 14% of all cases

41   involved sports or shoulder/elbow pathology.7 The most common cause for litigation involving

42   orthopedic sports procedures are pain and suffering, the need for multiple procedures and

43   neurovascular injury.8 However, this risk is not isolated to orthopedic surgeons with other
                                       Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


44   physicians providing game coverage, clearance for sports or return to play facing similar

45   medicolegal challenges and liability in caring for athletes.13, 14

46          Recent high profile settlements involving professional athletes generated debate and

47   concern regarding the perilous professional and medical-legal environment for physicians caring

48   for athletes. In February 2023, a former National Football League athlete was awarded 43.5

49   million dollars related to treatment of a PCL injury at the age of 30.5 Another Former NFL player

50   was awarded 28.5 million dollars after treatment for an ankle fracture sustained while playing on

51
                                                                      of
     a four-year 2.3 million dollar contract with the New York Giants in 2014.4 Similarly, there are

52
                                                               ro
     national trends across all United States lawsuits where cases that resulted in verdicts exceeding

53
                                                        -p
     10 million dollars in indemnities, noneconomic damages exceed both punitive and economic

54
                                                 re
     damages combined in the majority of instances.19

55
                                        lP
            In response to these and other recent high-profile lawsuits, an open letter calling for

56                              na
     protection of team physicians and their unique interdisciplinary role in caring for athletes signed

     by 23 academic medical societies was published.1, 11 Despite these concerns, there is limited
57

58
                         ur
     research on the medical malpractice burden facing orthopedic surgeons in the treatment of

59
                 Jo
     athletes. The purpose of this study is to quantify and describe the trends in malpractice litigation

60   involving the care of athletes at the professional and collegiate level using a publicly available

61   database.

62   Materials and Methods:

63          Westlaw Precision is a database of United States legal cases, lawsuits and jury . It was

64   queried from January 1st, 1993 to December 31st, 2023. Cases and Jury verdicts were searched

65   using two keywords entries, the first being "Sport” and any of the following with the Boolean

66   operator “OR” “Orthopedic, Surgeon, Physician, Malpractice, Athlete” and the second being
                                       Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


67   “Athlete” and any of the following with the Boolean operator “OR” “Orthopedic, Surgeon,

68   Physician, Malpractice, Sport.” Filters related to medical malpractice were then applied. Cases

69   including care of athletes at all levels with damages related to their ability to participate in future

70   recreation and sports activities were included. Obstetrical injury cases were excluded.

71          Demographic factors of defendants and plaintiffs were recorded as were financial

72   rewards in cases in favor of the plaintiffs. Data was collected between February 3rd, 2023 and

73   November 14th, 2023. Financial indemnities were converted to inflation adjusted 2023 United

74
                                                                      of
     States Dollars (USD) using an online calculator provided by the Federal Reserve Bank of

75   Minneapolis.10
                                                               ro
76
                                                        -p
            Statistical analysis was performed using Graphpad prism v10.1.2 (GraphPad, San Diego,

77
                                                 re
     CA, USA). Univariate analysis was performed using Mann-Whitney U test for nonparametric

78                                      lP
     data. A linear regression was used for the inflation-adjusted cost of damages for cases found in

79

80
                                na
     favor of plaintiffs and the year of the lawsuit.

     Results:

81
                         ur
            Eighty-eight cases were identified in the search. The majority involved were male

82               Jo
     athletes (n=66) who were adult (n=41) and with a mean age of 23.1 years.(Table 1) Football was

83   the most commonly represented sport (n=26). The most common level of play was high school

84   athletes (n=30). Among the defendant subspecialties orthopedics was the most prevalent (n=40.

85   (Table 1)

86          Thirty-seven cases were found in favor of the plaintiff with 28 jury verdicts, 6 settlements

87   and 4 arbitrations. (Table 2) Forty-five jury verdicts were in favor of the defendants. Remaining

88   case outcomes were not reported in the database or were reported as confidential. The sum of

89   reported indemnities exceeded 186 million 2023 USD, and football players represented 49% of
                                        Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


 90   these damages. College and professional athletes represented 16% and 42% of total financial

 91   indemnities respectively. (Table 2)

 92          Univariate analysis of demographics found only higher levels of play associated with

 93   higher median damages awarded. (Table 3) Defendant specialty, plaintiff sex, participation in

 94   football, wrongful death, or adult or pediatric age was not found to be statistically significant.

 95   (Table 3) Linear regression analysis showed an increasing trend in the inflation-adjusted cost of

 96   financial awards to plaintiffs (p=0.014). (Figure 1)

 97   Discussion:
                                                                       of
 98
                                                                ro
             Our study showed players at a professional or collegiate level involved in medical

 99
                                                         -p
      malpractice litigation commanded higher indemnities than other malpractice lawsuits involving

100
                                                  re
      athletes. No other plaintiff or defendant demographic in this study was associated with a

101                                      lP
      difference in inflation-adjusted indemnities. There was also a significant increasing trend in the

102

103
                                 na
      size of damages awarded over the last 30 years.

             In this study the majority of cases were found in favor of the defendant, which is

104
                          ur
      consistent with previous work published on malpractice lawsuits involving orthopedic surgeon

105               Jo
      malpractice6, 8 and sports-related spine injuries.22 Additionally, orthopedic surgeons and surgical

106   specialties, were not associated with higher indemnities in cases decided in favor of plaintiffs

107   when compared to other medical providers. This held true even though over half of the cases

108   found in favor of plaintiffs were lawsuits against orthopedic surgeons. Previous work has shown

109   orthopedic surgery is associated with a high burden of medical malpractice litigation,9 with the

110   majority of orthopedic surgeons being involved in at least one malpractice legal action over their

111   career.7, 9, 16, 17 Additionally, since 1988, the frequency of orthopedic malpractice legal action has

112   increased over 200%.7 Our study suggests that the increasing liability found in providing care for
                                         Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


113   high level athletes is not restricted to orthopedic surgeons, but may contribute to the already high

114   risk associated with orthopedic practice. Forty five percent of all lawsuits in our study involved

115   orthopedic physicians. (Table 1) There are an estimated 29,000 orthopedic surgeons practicing

116   in the United States12 making up approximately 3% of the total 950,000 practicing physician

117   workforce in the United States. 21 This represents a 15-fold increase in exposure to litigation in

118   the care of athletes for orthopedic surgeons compared to other providers.

119           In the 37 cases with awards reported to the plaintiff, the total cost of settlements in the

120
                                                                        of
      care of athletes from 1992-2023 in 2023 inflation adjusted dollars was $186,612,214. This is a

121
                                                                 ro
      relatively small sum compared to the 4 billion dollars annually in direct cost associated with

122
                                                          -p
      malpractice indemnities and settlements in the United States.3, 16-18, 20 However the average

123
                                                   re
      award was in excess of 5 million dollars and the largest was 43.5 million. By comparison, the

124                                       lP
      mean payout for orthopedic medical malpractice lawsuits across all subspecialties and patients in

      the United States has been reported between $898,972 -$1,374,640.7, 16 Settlements of this size
125

126
                                  na
      can create existential threats to independent practitioners or smaller institutions.2, 11, 19 It is also

127
                           ur
      unclear how this affects resource utilization and medical decision-making in healthcare systems

128                Jo
      participating the care of high level athletes and the physician-athlete relationship.

129           Shoulder and elbow surgeons should consider the impact of the care of athletes in their

130   malpractice liability. In a study of 25 medical malpractice lawsuits involving shoulder and

131   elbow surgery between 2010-2020 Sharma et al18 found the mean payout to be $4,058,952. The

132   average indemnity for athletes in our study was higher at $5,314,867 in 2023 inflation adjusted

133   dollars for the 3 cases found in favor of the plaintiff. (Table 2) Unfortunately this study suggests

134   treatment of high level athletes carries increasing malpractice liability for surgeons.
                                       Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


135           As surgeons assume greater financial risk in the care of professional athletes, potentially

136   injurious biases or hesitancies in treatment of athletes may be introduced. These concerns were

137   highlighted in the open letter published in June of 2023 by the American Orthopaedic Society for

138   Sports Medicine stating “litigation may have an enormous negative impact on the medical care

139   of competitive and elite athletes.”1 In the foreseeable future physicians may electively choose to

140   limit exposure to this increasing financial liability. This may occur by physicians willingly

141   reducing involvement in care of professional athletes, or at the behest of their employing hospital

142
                                                                      of
      and academic institutions seeking to reduce or avoid partnerships with teams to mitigate

143
                                                               ro
      economic risk. An alternative strategy is institutions requesting that athletes sign waivers that

144
                                                        -p
      limit awards or prescribe where a medical malpractice case can be tried. All of this may hamper

145
                                                 re
      the subspecialized and multidisciplinary care required for the treatment of injured high

146                                     lP
      performing athletes. Concerned physicians may consider collaborating with administrative

147

148
                                na
      leadership regarding the creation of ethical policies and procedures around any waivers for the

      care of athletes designed to mitigate financial risk. However, any such waiver may not be

149
                          ur
      enforceable and the authors are not aware of any related medical malpractice case law precedent

150                   Jo
      within the United States. As modern high level athletes frequently compete internationally

151   travelling the globe,15 physicians and medical professional societies both in the United States and

152   internationally should consider advocacy for additional legal protections or limitations on

153   malpractice award. This would be designed to avoid “nuclear verdicts”19 where a single lawsuit’s

154   exorbitant financial indemnity threatens closure or restructuring of medical practices and

155   institutions.

156           Limitations of this study include those inherent to retrospective and database studies.

157   Westlaw may not contain all lawsuits related to the malpractice and the care of athletes, and
                                       Increasing Cost in Caring for Athletes


158   entries may not be complete or contain keywords to be accurately included in this study.

159   Additionally, lawsuits involving high performing athletes are relatively rare due to the low

160   number of professional athletes nationwide and their likelihood of having an adverse outcome

161   from care prompting a malpractice claim.

162   Conclusions

163           There is a trend towards increasingly large damage claims over the last 30 years in

164   malpractice lawsuits involving athletes, particularly in the care of collegiate and professional

165
                                                                      of
      level players. This is concerning for possible erosion of the close working relationship of many

166
                                                                ro
      shoulder and elbow surgeons and other physicians with athletes and sports teams.1, 11 Future

167
                                                        -p
      work is needed to identify measures to increase communication, trust and patient satisfaction in

168
                                                 re
      athletes receiving care, and systems for financial protections for physicians facing inordinately

169   large financial indemnities.      lP

15	  Abstract
16	  Background: Non-contact injuries such as anterior cruciate ligament ruptures often occur during physical load
17	  toward the end of a match. This is ascribed to emerging processes due to exercise-induced fatigue. Moreover, non-
18	  contact injuries often occur during dynamic actions such as landing or cutting movements. Inter-limb asymmetries
19	  are suggested as one possible cause for those injuries based on findings indicating that asymmetries between
20	  limbs are associated with a higher injury risk. Hence, assessing inter-limb asymmetry during physical load in the
21	  condition of exercise-induced fatigue is warranted to identify potentially relevant precursors for non-contact
22	  injuries.
23	  Objective: The objective of this study was to overview the current state of evidence concerning the influence of
24	  exercise-induced fatigue on inter-limb asymmetries through a systematic review.
25	  Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted using the databases Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed,
26	  SURF, and SPONET to identify studies that assessed inter-limb asymmetries of healthy people, calculated with an
27	  asymmetry equation, before and after, or during a loading protocol.
28	  Results: Thirteen studies were included in the systematic review. The loading protocols involved running, race
29	  walking, jumping, squatting, soccer, rowing, and combinations of different exercises. Moreover, different tasks/
30	  procedures were used to assess inter-limb asymmetries, e.g., squats, single-leg countermovement jumps, gait
31	  analysis, or isokinetic strength testing. The results seem to depend on the implemented loading protocol, the tasks/
32	  procedures, and the measured parameters.
33	  Conclusions: Future research needs more systematization and consistency, assessing the effect of exercise-induced
34	  fatigue on inter-limb asymmetries. Moreover, the emergence of inter-limb asymmetries should be regarded in the
35	  context of sport-specific movements/tasks. Testing before, after, and during a physical loading protocol is advisable
36	  to consider the influence of exercise-induced fatigue on sport-specific tasks and to identify the possible
37	  mechanisms underlying load-dependent inter-limb asymmetries with regard to risk of non-contact injury.
38	  Keywords: Physical load, Injuries, Biomechanics, Side-to-side differences

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW                                                                                                                                    Open Access

The Influence of Exercise-Induced Fatigue
on Inter-Limb Asymmetries: a Systematic
Review
Jessica Heil* , Florian Loffing               and Dirk Büsch


  Abstract
  Background: Non-contact injuries such as anterior cruciate ligament ruptures often occur during physical load
  toward the end of a match. This is ascribed to emerging processes due to exercise-induced fatigue. Moreover, non-
  contact injuries often occur during dynamic actions such as landing or cutting movements. Inter-limb asymmetries
  are suggested as one possible cause for those injuries based on findings indicating that asymmetries between
  limbs are associated with a higher injury risk. Hence, assessing inter-limb asymmetry during physical load in the
  condition of exercise-induced fatigue is warranted to identify potentially relevant precursors for non-contact
  injuries.
  Objective: The objective of this study was to overview the current state of evidence concerning the influence of
  exercise-induced fatigue on inter-limb asymmetries through a systematic review.
  Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted using the databases Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed,
  SURF, and SPONET to identify studies that assessed inter-limb asymmetries of healthy people, calculated with an
  asymmetry equation, before and after, or during a loading protocol.
  Results: Thirteen studies were included in the systematic review. The loading protocols involved running, race
  walking, jumping, squatting, soccer, rowing, and combinations of different exercises. Moreover, different tasks/
  procedures were used to assess inter-limb asymmetries, e.g., squats, single-leg countermovement jumps, gait
  analysis, or isokinetic strength testing. The results seem to depend on the implemented loading protocol, the tasks/
  procedures, and the measured parameters.
  Conclusions: Future research needs more systematization and consistency, assessing the effect of exercise-induced
  fatigue on inter-limb asymmetries. Moreover, the emergence of inter-limb asymmetries should be regarded in the
  context of sport-specific movements/tasks. Testing before, after, and during a physical loading protocol is advisable
  to consider the influence of exercise-induced fatigue on sport-specific tasks and to identify the possible
  mechanisms underlying load-dependent inter-limb asymmetries with regard to risk of non-contact injury.
  Keywords: Physical load, Injuries, Biomechanics, Side-to-side differences

28	                                      months post-ACLR) assessing LD influence on knee extension and flexion peak torque, center of pressure (COP) distance and

30	                                      indicator variables and categorized as “Pass” or “Fail” based on LSI ≥ 90%.

34	                                      outcomes; NDL was more symmetric during COP distance tests (P = 0.03, d = 0.40). No differences were observed between

36	                                      limb for triple-hop (P = 0.03, d = 0.23) but not single-hop (P > 0.05) distance.

38	                                      higher symmetry and a greater rate of LSI Pass success for knee extension strength.

                                      The Influence of Limb Dominance on
                                      Performance-Based Outcomes After
                                      ACL Reconstruction
                                      Jordan Hodges, BS, Amelia S. Bruce Leicht, PhD, CSCS,*
                                      Xavier D. Thompson, PhD, ATC, Brian C. Werner, MD, David R. Diduch, MD,
                                      Stephen F. Brockmeier, MD, and Joe M. Hart, PhD, ATC


                                      Background: Considering limb dominance (LD) may be valuable when utilizing limb symmetry index (LSI) when assessing
                                      patients after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR).
                                      Hypothesis: Patients will have better performance-based outcomes when index ACLR occurred on the dominant limb (DL)
                                      compared with the nondominant limb (NDL).
                                      Study Design: Observational cross-sectional study.
                                      Level of Evidence: Level 3.
                                      Methods: A total of 279 patients (49.1% female, 20.83 ± 5.23 years; 48% DL surgery) completed a laboratory visit (7.65 ± 1.65
                                      months post-ACLR) assessing LD influence on knee extension and flexion peak torque, center of pressure (COP) distance and
                                      velocity, and hop performance. LD was defined as the preferred limb to kick a soccer ball. LSI variables were converted to
                                      indicator variables and categorized as “Pass” or “Fail” based on LSI ≥ 90%.
                                      Results: Patient LD and isometric knee extension LSI Pass status were significantly associated (χ2 = 10.09; P = 0.001).
                                      No additional associations were found between LD and other LSI Pass status variables (P > 0.05). Patients with DL ACLR
                                      demonstrated more symmetric knee extension peak torque (P < 0.001, d = 0.42) and 6-meter hop (P = 0.02, d = 0.25)
                                      outcomes; NDL was more symmetric during COP distance tests (P = 0.03, d = 0.40). No differences were observed between
                                      LD and raw strength or balance measures (P > 0.05). Patients with ACLR on their NDL jumped farther on their contralateral
                                      limb for triple-hop (P = 0.03, d = 0.23) but not single-hop (P > 0.05) distance.
                                      Conclusion: LD appears to influence isometric knee LSI in patients post-ACLR; patients with surgery on their DL achieved
                                      higher symmetry and a greater rate of LSI Pass success for knee extension strength.
                                      Clinical Relevance: Addressing differences in recovery patterns between DL and NDL may improve rehabilitation
                                      precision and guide return-to-activity timelines after ACLR.
                                      Keywords: limb dominance; limb symmetry index; return to activity (RTA)

 "sourceFile":"The influence of movement tempo on acute neuromuscular, hormonal, and mechanical responses to resistance exercise - A mini review.pdf",
 "decision":"DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"The article's own DOI is not printed anywhere in the extracted text (no DOI string appears in the body, header or footer; the reference list contains none for this article). Content is complete and readable.",
 "doiMissing":true,
 "identityCheck":"The title in the text, The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise-A Mini Review, matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A mini review of acute studies on movement tempo in isotonic resistance exercise, based on a keyword search of seven databases and inclusion of peer-reviewed studies in healthy adults. The included studies, which had 6 to 42 participants each and were mostly resistance-trained men, showed that slower tempos reduced the repetitions possible at a given load and the 1RM in several studies, while total time under tension rose with slower tempos. Lactate, testosterone, growth hormone and cortisol responses were inconsistent across studies.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The search and selection are described briefly, with no counts of records screened and no pooled analysis, so the conclusions are a narrative synthesis. The included studies are small and differ in load, tempo, exercise and outcome, and most designs cannot separate eccentric from concentric effects.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat slower tempo as a reliable driver of hormone and lactate responses, but the authors report that these findings conflict across studies and that tempo effects have not been tested in athletes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Wilk M, Tufano JJ, Zajac A. The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise: A Mini Review. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020;34(8):2369-2383.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"The review describes how premeditated movement tempo affects resistance training variables. Slower tempos reduce the 1RM, the load that can be used, and the number of repetitions performed at a given load, while increasing total time under tension, which can influence acute cardiovascular and hormonal responses. The authors suggest testing maximal strength and repetitions at each tempo used, because programming tempo without this testing is closer to trial and error.",
   "tldr":"Slower lifting tempos lower the repetitions possible and the 1RM, and increase total time under tension, but hormone and lactate responses vary between studies. Test 1RM at each tempo you plan to use, and track total time under tension as part of training volume.",
   "methods":"A mini review searched Google Scholar, MEDLINE, ADONIS, ERIC, SPORTDiscus, EBSCOhost and PubMed with paired keyword terms on tempo, time under tension, volume and acute responses. Included studies were original peer-reviewed English-language research in healthy adults that used isotonic resistance exercise, with no sex restriction. The authors also set a tempo classification (volitional, explosive, fast, medium, slow and extremely slow) and summarized each study's tempo, load, sample and findings.",
   "findings":"Slower tempos were associated with fewer repetitions at a given load in several studies and with lower 1RM in one study (about 3.7% lower with a 4/0/2/0 than a 2/0/2/0 tempo). Total time under tension increased with slower tempos, for example 178.8 s for 6/0/4/0 versus 124.65 s for 2/0/2/0 over five sets. Blood lactate, testosterone, growth hormone and cortisol responses were inconsistent across studies, with some finding greater responses at slower tempos and others finding no difference.",
   "limitations":"The authors note that most included studies cannot separate the effects of eccentric and concentric duration, and that load, volume, rest and exercise often differ between tempo conditions. The review does not pool results, and the studies are small and mostly in men or resistance-trained participants. Several conclusions are described by the authors as speculative and in need of further research.",
   "practicalImplications":"Test 1RM at each tempo used, since slower tempos reduce the load and repetitions that can be lifted, and set training loads from that test. Track total time under tension as well as repetitions when judging volume. The authors suggest slower tempos for controlled, time-under-tension work and faster concentric movement for power, and note that tempo can vary between sessions, sets or exercises.",
   "athleteDev":"Tempo changes the load, repetitions and total time under tension, so programs that specify tempo should base loads on a 1RM tested at that tempo. The authors suggest slower tempos may suit youth or injured athletes, but they do not test this and the review found no data on tempo effects on power output in athletes.",
   "rtp":"The review mentions injured athletes only as a suggestion that controlled tempos may help manage load, and it reports no rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes. It cannot show that tempo training speeds return to sport or lowers reinjury risk."
 }
}

Responses to Resistance Exercise—A Mini Review

Abstract
Wilk, M, Tufano, JJ, and Zajac, A. The influence of movement tempo on acute neuromuscular, hormonal, and mechanical
responses to resistance exercise—a mini review. J Strength Cond Res 34(8): 2369–2383, 2020—Resistance training studies
mainly analyze variables such as the type and order of exercise, intensity, number of sets, number of repetitions, and duration and
frequency of rest periods. However, one variable that is often overlooked in resistance training research, as well as in practice, is
premeditated movement tempo, which can influence a myriad of mechanical and physiological factors associated with training and
adaptation. Specifically, this article provides an overview of the available scientific literature and describes how slower tempos
negatively affect the 1-repetition maximum, the possible load to be used, and the number of repetitions performed with a given load,
while also increasing the total time under tension, which can mediate acute cardiovascular and hormonal responses. As a result,
coaches should consider testing maximal strength and the maximal number of repetitions that can be performed with each
movement tempo that is to be used during training. Otherwise, programming resistance training using various movement tempos is
more of a trial-and-error approach, rather than being evidence or practice based. Furthermore, practical applications are provided
to show how movement tempo can be adjusted for a variety of case study–type scenarios.
Key Words: repetitions, time under tension, 1RM test, testosterone, cortisol, growth hormone

{
 "id": "Q14",
 "sourceFile": "The influence of psychological factors on the incidence and severity of sports-related concussions - A systematic review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, The Influence of Psychological Factors on the Incidence and Severity of Sports-Related Concussions: A Systematic Review, matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": [
  "Brain Health & Psychology",
  "Sports Medicine & Injury"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Research & Analytics"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport",
  "American Football",
  "Soccer",
  "Rugby"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Mixed / Unspecified",
  "Youth / Adolescent",
  "Collegiate",
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Injured Athletes",
  "Male Athletes",
  "Female Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "A PRISMA systematic review, registered in PROSPERO, of 10 studies on preexisting psychological factors and sports-related concussion in athletes of all sports, with samples from about 40 to 1,246 athletes, mostly male. The authors report that meanness, aggression and psychoticism were linked to more concussions in one study of male football players, and that baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms were linked to worse symptoms after concussion. No meta-analysis was done because the study designs were heterogeneous, and the certainty of evidence was rated low to moderate.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Most incidence findings come from one study of male football players, and several studies relied on self-reported concussion history that may be inaccurate. The included studies differ in samples, measures and designs, so the associations cannot be used to predict concussion for an individual athlete.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could use these traits to screen athletes for concussion risk, but the authors say the associations are unclear and rest on heterogeneous, mostly small studies.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2019,
  "citation": "Trinh LN, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK. The Influence of Psychological Factors on the Incidence and Severity of Sports-Related Concussions: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019:1-9.",
  "doi": "10.1177/0363546519882626",
  "abstract": "A systematic review, following PRISMA, of studies on whether preexisting emotional states, personality traits, temperament, life stressors and explanatory style affect the incidence and severity of sports-related concussion in athletes. Meanness, aggression and psychoticism were associated with more concussions, baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms with worse symptoms after concussion, and psychiatric illness, family history and life stressors with postconcussion syndrome in young athletes. The authors rate the evidence as low to moderate certainty.",
  "tldr": "Some preexisting traits, such as meanness, aggression and psychoticism, were linked to more concussions in one study of football players, and baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms were linked to worse symptoms after concussion. Certainty is low to moderate, so these traits are not yet useful for screening individual athletes.",
  "methods": "A PRISMA-guided search of PubMed, Embase, Medline and ScienceDirect, plus reference lists, covered English-language studies on preexisting psychological factors and concussion incidence or symptoms. Ten studies met inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively, because the designs were too heterogeneous for a meta-analysis. The review was registered with PROSPERO.",
  "findings": "In 917 male football players, higher baseline negative emotionality, psychoticism, meanness, anger and aggression were associated with more concussions, and in collegiate athletes higher agreeableness was associated with more unreported concussions. Higher baseline emotional or depressive symptoms were associated with worse post-concussion symptoms in two studies, and psychiatric illness, family history and life stressors were more common in young athletes (n=40) who developed postconcussion syndrome. Explanatory style was not associated with concussion incidence, but optimism was associated with longer recovery from complex concussions in one study.",
  "limitations": "The patient groups and measures are heterogeneous, and some studies relied on self-reported concussion history, which may be inaccurate or underreported. Most participants were male, and many studies did not report incidence by sex. The conclusion lists pessimism among factors linked to higher incidence, but the explanatory style study found no incidence difference by optimism or pessimism, so the conclusion does not match the results.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes who report higher baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness or depressive symptoms may warrant closer monitoring after a concussion, as the authors suggest. A psychiatric history, family history or significant life stressors may flag young athletes at higher risk of postconcussion syndrome. The authors suggest baseline psychological screening could help prevention and management, but the review does not test that.",
  "athleteDev": "This review does not inform training or performance programming. Its only performance-linked finding is that extraversion and height predicted heading frequency in male soccer players, which does not set a training target.",
  "rtp": "The review gives only general guidance for return to play: baseline emotional symptoms and psychiatric history may relate to post-concussion symptoms, and optimism was linked to longer recovery from complex concussions in one study. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance."
 }
}

  "abstract": "A systematic review, following PRISMA, of studies on whether preexisting emotional states, personality traits, temperament, life stressors and explanatory style affect the incidence and severity of sports-related concussion in athletes. Meanness, aggression and psychoticism were associated with more concussions, baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms with worse symptoms after concussion, and psychiatric illness, family history and life stressors with postconcussion syndrome in young athletes. The authors rate the evidence as low to moderate certainty.",
  "tldr": "Some preexisting traits, such as meanness, aggression and psychoticism, were linked to more concussions in one study of football players, and baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms were linked to worse symptoms after concussion. Certainty is low to moderate, so these traits are not yet useful for screening individual athletes.",
  "methods": "A PRISMA-guided search of PubMed, Embase, Medline and ScienceDirect, plus reference lists, covered English-language studies on preexisting psychological factors and concussion incidence or symptoms. Ten studies met inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively, because the designs were too heterogeneous for a meta-analysis. The review was registered with PROSPERO.",
  "findings": "In 917 male football players, higher baseline negative emotionality, psychoticism, meanness, anger and aggression were associated with more concussions, and in collegiate athletes higher agreeableness was associated with more unreported concussions. Higher baseline emotional or depressive symptoms were associated with worse post-concussion symptoms in two studies, and psychiatric illness, family history and life stressors were more common in young athletes (n=40) who developed postconcussion syndrome. Explanatory style was not associated with concussion incidence, but optimism was associated with longer recovery from complex concussions in one study.",
  "limitations": "The patient groups and measures are heterogeneous, and some studies relied on self-reported concussion history, which may be inaccurate or underreported. Most participants were male, and many studies did not report incidence by sex. The conclusion lists pessimism among factors linked to higher incidence, but the explanatory style study found no incidence difference by optimism or pessimism, so the conclusion does not match the results.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes who report higher baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness or depressive symptoms may warrant closer monitoring after a concussion, as the authors suggest. A psychiatric history, family history or significant life stressors may flag young athletes at higher risk of postconcussion syndrome. The authors suggest baseline psychological screening could help prevention and management, but the review does not test that.",
  "athleteDev": "This review does not inform training or performance programming. Its only performance-linked finding is that extraversion and height predicted heading frequency in male soccer players, which does not set a training target.",
  "rtp": "The review gives only general guidance for return to play: baseline emotional symptoms and psychiatric history may relate to post-concussion symptoms, and optimism was linked to longer recovery from complex concussions in one study. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance."

5	on the Incidence and Severity
6	of Sports-Related Concussions
7	A Systematic Review
8	Lily N. Trinh,* BS, Symone M. Brown,y MPH, and Mary K. Mulcahey,yz MD
9	Investigation performed at Tulane University School of Medicine, New Orleans, Louisiana, USA
10	
11	Background: An athlete’s preexisting psychological factors may influence the incidence and/or severity of sports-related con-
12	cussions (SRCs).
13	Purpose: To determine if emotional states, personality traits, temperament, life stressors, and explanatory styles (optimism vs
14	pessimism) influence the incidence and severity of SRCs in athletes.
15	Study Design: Systematic review.
16	Methods: A systematic literature search of multiple major medical reference databases was performed following the PRISMA
17	(Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. Studies were included that evaluated the
18	effect of preexisting psychological factors on the incidence and severity of SRCs in male and female athletes participating in
19	all sports.
20	Results: The initial search identified 1195 articles. Ten studies met our inclusion criteria and were included in our analysis. Factors
21	such as meanness, aggression, and psychoticism were associated with an increased incidence of SRCs. Baseline traits of irri-
22	tability, sadness, nervousness, and depressive symptoms were associated with worse symptomatology after SRCs. In young ath-
23	letes, preexisting psychiatric illnesses, family history of psychiatric illness, and significant life stressors were associated with an
24	increased risk of developing postconcussion syndrome after SRCs.
25	Conclusion: This systematic review demonstrated a potential relationship between an athlete’s preexisting psychological factors
26	and the incidence and severity of SRCs. These associations are not entirely clear owing to the heterogeneity across included
27	studies and the low-to-moderate certainty of evidence. Future studies should attempt to evaluate men and women independently,
28	use well-validated psychological questionnaires, and limit the usage of self-reported SRCs, when possible. Furthermore, the
29	potential efficacy of baseline psychological factor and/or symptom reports on the prevention and management of SRCs should
30	be explored.
31	Keywords: sports-related concussion; psychological factors; sports injury; psychology

The Influence of Psychological Factors
on the Incidence and Severity
of Sports-Related Concussions
A Systematic Review
Lily N. Trinh,* BS, Symone M. Brown,y MPH, and Mary K. Mulcahey,yz MD
Investigation performed at Tulane University School of Medicine, New Orleans, Louisiana, USA

Background: An athlete’s preexisting psychological factors may influence the incidence and/or severity of sports-related con-
cussions (SRCs).
Purpose: To determine if emotional states, personality traits, temperament, life stressors, and explanatory styles (optimism vs
pessimism) influence the incidence and severity of SRCs in athletes.
Study Design: Systematic review.
Methods: A systematic literature search of multiple major medical reference databases was performed following the PRISMA
(Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. Studies were included that evaluated the
effect of preexisting psychological factors on the incidence and severity of SRCs in male and female athletes participating in
all sports.
Results: The initial search identified 1195 articles. Ten studies met our inclusion criteria and were included in our analysis. Factors
such as meanness, aggression, and psychoticism were associated with an increased incidence of SRCs. Baseline traits of irri-
tability, sadness, nervousness, and depressive symptoms were associated with worse symptomatology after SRCs. In young ath-
letes, preexisting psychiatric illnesses, family history of psychiatric illness, and significant life stressors were associated with an
increased risk of developing postconcussion syndrome after SRCs.
Conclusion: This systematic review demonstrated a potential relationship between an athlete’s preexisting psychological factors
and the incidence and severity of SRCs. These associations are not entirely clear owing to the heterogeneity across included
studies and the low-to-moderate certainty of evidence. Future studies should attempt to evaluate men and women independently,
use well-validated psychological questionnaires, and limit the usage of self-reported SRCs, when possible. Furthermore, the
potential efficacy of baseline psychological factor and/or symptom reports on the prevention and management of SRCs should
be explored.
Keywords: sports-related concussion; psychological factors; sports injury; psychology

{
 "id": "Q15",
 "sourceFile": "The injury mechanism of Achilles tendon rupture in professional athletes - A video analysis study.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, The Injury Mechanism of Achilles Tendon Rupture in Professional Athletes: A Video Analysis Study, matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Case Report / Case Series",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Rehabilitation"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Basketball",
  "American Football",
  "Soccer",
  "Baseball / Softball",
  "Rugby"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Injured Athletes",
  "Male Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "A retrospective observational series of 42 Achilles tendon ruptures in professional athletes (41 men and 1 woman, mean age 28.4 years; 18 basketball, 14 American football, 5 soccer, 3 baseball and 2 rugby players), analyzed from publicly available videos. Of the ruptures, 83.3% were noncontact, the most frequent game activities were take-off or acceleration (40.5%) and stop or rotate (38.1%), and at rupture the ankle was dorsiflexed in 71.4% and the trunk flexed in 73.8%. Three reviewers showed high agreement (Fleiss kappa above 0.864 intraobserver and above 0.815 interobserver).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Videos were non-standardized, so joint angles were not measured and positions are qualitative. Cases came from public online sources that may be incomplete or inaccurate, the sample is small, and it is mostly basketball and men, with no comparison group of uninjured athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the posture at rupture as a cause that drills can prevent, but the study only describes positions in a series of public videos and does not show that any position or drill changes rupture risk.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Yüce A, Yerli M, Misir A. The Injury Mechanism of Achilles Tendon Rupture in Professional Athletes: A Video Analysis Study. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2024;114(3).",
  "doi": "10.7547/21-196",
  "abstract": "The study used video analysis to describe how Achilles tendon ruptures occur in professional athletes and what body posture is present at the time of injury. Of 42 analyzed injuries, most occurred during take-off or acceleration, or during stopping and turning. At rupture, the ankle was in dorsiflexion, the body was bent forward, and the knee and hip were in extension. The authors suggest the findings can guide neuromuscular, proprioceptive and balance training to prevent rupture.",
  "tldr": "In this series of 42 professional-athlete ruptures, most happened without contact during take-off, acceleration or stopping and turning, with the ankle dorsiflexed and the trunk flexed. These movements can guide prevention drills, but the sample is small and based on public videos.",
  "methods": "A retrospective observational study identified 114 Achilles ruptures in professional athletes from 1970 to 2020 through internet searches. Of 48 videos accessed, 42 with adequate quality were analyzed by three reviewers who had not previously done video analysis and who scored each video blindly for contact, game activity and body position. Agreement was assessed with Fleiss kappa, and joint angles were not measured because the videos were not standardized.",
  "findings": "Of the 42 athletes, 35 (83.3%) had noncontact injuries, and the most frequent game activities were take-off or acceleration (40.5%), stop or rotate (38.1%) and landing (16.7%). At rupture, the ankle was dorsiflexed in 71.4%, the trunk was flexed in 73.8%, and the hip and knee were extended in 61.9% and 54.8% of cases. Intraobserver agreement was above 0.864 and interobserver agreement above 0.815.",
  "limitations": "Videos came from different platforms with different angles and quality, so joint angles could not be measured and only qualitative positions were recorded. Injury data came from public records that may not be complete or accurate, and the sample is small, almost all male, and led by basketball players (18 of 42). The abstract and discussion give 38.5% for stop or turn, while Table 2 gives 38.1% (16 of 42).",
  "practicalImplications": "The common activities (take-off, acceleration, stopping and turning) and the posture at rupture (ankle dorsiflexed, trunk flexed, knee and hip extended) can guide which movements to include in neuromuscular, balance and proprioceptive training. The authors also suggest sport-specific conditioning and strengthening, but the study did not test whether these reduce rupture rates.",
  "athleteDev": "The take-off, acceleration and stop-and-turn positions can guide sport-specific neuromuscular and balance drills, particularly for basketball players, who were 18 of the 42 cases. The study does not measure performance outcomes or show that these drills prevent ruptures.",
  "rtp": "The study does not inform return to sport. It does not report rehabilitation methods, surgical treatment or return-to-play criteria, although it notes that many athletes fail to return to their previous level. Its findings may help choose movements for prevention work, but they cannot guide clearance decisions."
 }
}

ORIGINAL ARTICLES

The Injury Mechanism of Achilles Tendon Rupture in
Professional Athletes
A Video Analysis Study
Ali Yüce, MD*
Mustafa Yerli, MD*
Abdulhamit Misir, MD†

Background: In professional athletes, Achilles tendon ruptures are devastating injuries, of-
ten resulting in season loss or decreased return to sports level. We aimed to perform a com-
prehensive video analysis to describe the mechanisms of Achilles tendon rupture as well as
body posture in professional athletes. We hypothesized that Achilles tendon ruptures in pro-
fessional athletes develop with a speciﬁc injury mechanism and that body posture at the
time of injury varies by sport.
Methods: Of 114 identiﬁed Achilles tendon ruptures that occurred in professional athletes
between 1970 and 2020, 42 with adequate video data were analyzed for injury mechanism,
body posture, and player and sport characteristics by three independent reviewers.
Results: Mean 6 SD age of the 42 athletes (41 men and 1 woman) was 28.4 6 4.26 years.
Eighteen athletes played basketball (42.9%), 14 football (33.3%), ﬁve soccer (11.9%), three
baseball (7.1%), and two rugby (4.8%). Thirty-ﬁve patients (83.3%) had noncontact injuries.
The most frequent months of injury were January (16.7%) and October (14.3%). During
Achilles tendon rupture, the ankle was in dorsiﬂexion, the body was bent forward, the knee
and hip were in extension, and the foot was in a neutral position. Most injuries occurred dur-
ing take-off/acceleration (40.5%) or stop and turn (38.5%) maneuvers.
Conclusions: In professional athletes, the Achilles tendon most often ruptures during take-
off/acceleration. The most common position during rupture is the trunk in ﬂexion, the knee
and hip in extension, and the ankle in dorsiﬂexion. This information can guide professional
athletes in terms of physical therapy techniques, including neuromuscular training, proprio-
ception, and balance training speciﬁc to preventing Achilles tendon rupture. (J Am Podiatr
Med Assoc 114(3), 2024; doi:10.7547/21-196)

 "id":"Q16",
 "sourceFile":"The injury rate in NFL players was increased following cancellation of preseason games due to COVID-19.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title in the text, The Injury Rate in NFL Players was Increased Following Cancellation of Preseason Games due to COVID 19, matches the filename (hyphen and spacing differ only).",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A retrospective review of 3,025 NFL injuries in publicly reported injury reports across four seasons, with rates calculated per 1,000 athlete exposures. Injury rates in weeks 1 to 4 of the 2020 regular season (5.2, 5.9, 5.0 and 5.4 per 1,000) were higher than the same weeks of the 2016 to 2019 regular seasons (2.8, 4.5, 3.3 and 3.6), with relative risks of 1.31 to 1.88 and P values of 0.01 or lower; the 2020 preseason had been cancelled. The authors attribute the rise to deconditioning and fatigue, which they did not measure.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Public injury reports may be incomplete or inaccurate, and injury severity, diagnosis and games missed for 2020 were not available. Denominators assume fixed roster sizes (90, 75 and 53 players) for all 32 teams, and the design cannot separate the cancelled preseason from other pandemic-era changes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this as showing that a cancelled preseason causes higher injury rates, but the study measures neither conditioning nor fatigue, and the authors themselves say the pandemic limits how the finding should be read.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Baker HP, Pirkle S, Cahill M, Reddy M, Portney D, Athiviraham A. The Injury Rate in NFL Players was Increased Following Cancellation of Preseason Games due to COVID 19. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2021.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.asmr.2021.05.002",
   "abstract":"A retrospective review of NFL players placed on the injury report during preseason and the first four regular-season weeks from 2016-2017 to 2020-2021. Of 3,025 injuries, 582 occurred in weeks 1 to 4 of the 2020-2021 regular season, and the injury rate in those weeks was significantly higher than in the same period of three recent past seasons. The authors conclude that injury rates rose after preseason games were cancelled because of COVID-19.",
   "tldr":"Injury rates in weeks 1 to 4 of the 2020 NFL regular season were higher than in the same weeks of earlier seasons, after the preseason was cancelled. This public-record study cannot show cause, since it measured no conditioning or fatigue, so treat it as a signal rather than proof.",
   "methods":"A retrospective review used publicly available weekly injury reports from NFL.com, ESPN, CBS Sports, Pro-Football-Reference and Bleacher Report, with each injury checked against a missed game. Rates were calculated per 1,000 athlete exposures using roster sizes of 90 (preseason games 1 to 3), 75 (preseason game 4) and 53 (regular season) players across 32 teams. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals compared 2020 weeks 1 to 4 with the same weeks of prior seasons, using t tests and chi-square tests.",
   "findings":"Of 3,025 injuries over the study seasons, 582 occurred in weeks 1 to 4 of 2020 and 1,292 and 1,151 occurred in preseason and regular-season weeks 1 to 4 of earlier seasons. Regular-season rates in 2020 were 5.2, 5.9, 5.0 and 5.4 per 1,000 athlete exposures, compared with 2.8, 4.5, 3.3 and 3.6 in 2016 to 2019, with relative risks of 1.88, 1.31, 1.53 and 1.48 (P of 0.01 or lower). Knee (16%), hip or groin (11%) and ankle (10%) were the most common sites, and 71% of injuries were from player contact.",
   "limitations":"The data come from public records that may omit or misreport injuries, and injury severity, diagnosis and clearance were not available. The study did not measure deconditioning or fatigue, did not follow the 2020 season to its end, and cannot separate the cancelled preseason from other pandemic-era changes. Table 2 gives a relative risk of 4.09 for preseason week 4, which does not match its own rates (5.4 vs 1.9 gives 2.84), and the Results percentages for preseason (53%) do not share the 3,025 total (1,292 is 43%).",
   "practicalImplications":"A shortened or missing preseason may be followed by a higher early-season injury rate, which supports managing early-season workload closely. The authors suggest questionnaire-based fatigue and well-being monitoring to guide recovery and training, but this study did not test any monitoring tool or intervention.",
   "athleteDev":"Conditioning and load progression before the season matter more when preseason practice is limited. The authors speculate that deconditioning and fatigue explain the rise, but the study measured neither and tested no training intervention.",
   "rtp":"The study does not inform return to sport. It counts injuries and missed games for the early season but reports no injury severity, rehabilitation or clearance criteria, and games missed for 2020 were not available."
 }
