  1 Abstract

 2 Purpose: To investigate the injury rate in NFL athletes during the first four weeks of the 2020
 3 NFL season.

 4 Methods: This study was a retrospective review of all NFL players who were placed on the
 5 injury report during the preseason and first four weeks of the regular season from the 2016-2017
 6 through 2020-2021 NFL regular seasons. Player’s date of injury was cross-referenced with an
 7 absence of statistics from the respective games for which they were ruled out to ensure accuracy.
 8 Injury rates were calculated per 1000 athletic exposures (AE). Relative risk (RR) with 95%
 9 of
 confidence intervals (CI) compared injury rates between the two cohorts.

10
ro
 Results: Over the course of the study period of four NFL seasons 3025 injuries were reported.
11 -p
 Of the 3025 injuries reported, 582 (19%) occurred during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular
12
13
re
 season, while 1292 (53%) occurred during preseason weeks 1-4 and 1151 (38%) during regular
 seasons weeks 1-4 of NFL seasons 2016-2017, 2018-2019, and 2019-2020. There was a
14 lP
 significant increase in the injury rate during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular season for all
15
16
na
 comparisons with the injury rate both during the preseason and regular season of three recent
 past NFL seasons.

17
 ur
 Conclusions: The rate of injury in NFL players during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular
18
 Jo
 seasons was significantly higher than three recent past NFL preseasons and regular seasons.

19 Level of Evidence: Level IV, diagnostic case series.

20

21 Introduction

22 Due to rising number of positive Covid-19 tests observed in NFL players during the summer of
23 2020, the NFL suspended the 2020 preseason on July 21, 20201. Suspension of play out of
24 concern regarding rising cases of Covid-19 in the United States was widespread and not limited
25 to the NFL, similar trends were observed across all sports and levels including high school
26 collegiate, and professional. In order to mitigate potential Covid-19 exposures NFL team training
 27 camp roster sizes were limited to 80 players1. Typically, the NFL preseason serves as the
28 primary time for preparing athletes for the rigors of the upcoming NFL season. However, given
29 this unprecedented stoppage of preseason training and teams inability to continue with practice
30 and games due to social distancing precautions, athletes were forced to train and condition on
31 their own. We speculated that athletes, in the absence of organized team activities, developed
32 sports deconditioning.

33 Previous studies have demonstrated that fatigue and deconditioning may place athletes at a
34 higher risk for injury. The International Olympic Committee identified absolute load, calendar
35 congestion, and psychological load to be closely associated with injury risk through a variety of
36
of
 mechanisms.2 Excessive training that exceeds the body’s loadbearing capacity causes
37 ro
 microtrauma to tendons, muscles, and bones, which is the etiology of overuse injuries.3-8

38
-p
 In light of these findings highlighting the association between fatigue and risk of injury,
39 re
 investigating modifiable causes influencing athletes’ levels of fatigue is a critical step in
40 reducing risk of injury.
lP
41
42
na
 The purpose of this study was to investigate the injury rate in NFL athletes during the first four
 weeks of the 2020 NFL seasons. Our hypothesis was that the observed injury rate during the first
43 ur
 month of the 2020-2021 NFL season would be significantly higher when compared to past
44 seasons.
 Jo
45

46 Methods

47 Data collection

48 This study was a retrospective review of all NFL players who were placed on the injury report
49 during the preseason and first four weeks of the regular season from the 2016-2017 through
50 2020-2021 NFL regular seasons. The data was compiled using publicly available injury reports
51 (Appendix). The sources used publish a weekly injury reports detailing the name of the players
52 injured, their corresponding teams, and a brief description of each injury. At least two different
 53 sources were used to cross-reference injury information. To verify each player’s date of injury,
54 we confirmed each player’s reported injury date corresponded to an absence of statistics from the
55 respective games for which they were ruled out. These methods are in accordance with
56 previously published protocols.9-13 When collecting data, we noted that the 2017-2018 records
57 were incomplete, thus we excluded them from the study. We felt that data from three recent past
58 seasons to compare data from 2020 to was adequate.

59 Team records available on individual team websites were used to collect demographic
60 information. Our dataset included each player’s name, position, team, pathology, age at injury,
61 date of injury, season. Data for the 2020 season was collected prospectively, thus we were unable
62
of
 to determine games missed due to injury as the 2020 NFL season was ongoing when this
63 manuscript was written. ro
64 Definitions
-p
65
re
 Reportable injuries were based on the criteria that the injury necessitated a team physician
66 lP
 referral or emergent care and resulted in missed athletic activity. An athlete-exposure (AE) was
67
na
 defined as one athlete’s participation in one game in which they were exposed to potential injury.

68 ur
 Data and Statistical Analysis

69
70
 Jo
 Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 25 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, Illinois). Injury rates were
 calculated per 1000 AEs using the following calculations; for the first 3 preseason games where
71 NFL teams carry 90 players on the roster (Total number of injuries x 1000/ Total number of AEs
72 (AEs = 90 players * 32 NFL teams * number of games)); for the fourth preseason game where
73 NFL teams cut the roster to 75 players (Total number of injuries x 1000/ Total number of AEs
74 (AEs = 75 players * 32 NFL teams * number of games)); and for the regular season games (Total
75 number of injuries x 1000/ Total number of AEs (AEs = 53 players * 32 NFL teams * number of
76 games)). Risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) compared injury rates between the
77 two cohorts. Risk ratios were calculated comparing both weeks 1-4 from the preseason and
78 regular season of NFL seasons 2016-2017, 2018-2019, and 2019-2020 to the 2020-2021 season.
79 Week 1 of the 2020-2021 NFL season was compared to both past preseason and regular season
80 week 1, this method of comparison was continued for weeks 2-4. Continuous variables were
  81 statistically compared using two-tailed t-test, while categorical variables were compared using
 82 Chi-squared test. Statistical significance was set at P ≤ 0.05.

 83

 84 Results

 85 Over the course of the study period of four NFL seasons 3025 injuries were reported. Of the
 86 3025 injuries reported, 582 (19%) occurred during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular season,
 87 while 1292 (53%) occurred during preseason weeks 1-4 and 1151 (38%) during regular seasons
 88
 89
of
 weeks 1-4 of NFL seasons 2016-2017, 2018-2019, and 2019-2020 (Table 1 and Figure 1). There
 was a significant increase in the injury rate during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular season for
 90
ro
 all comparisons with the injury rate both during the preseason and regular season of three recent
 91 past NFL seasons (Table 2). -p
 92
re
 Positional breakdown demonstrated that wide receivers, safeties, and linebackers sustained the
 93
 94
lP
 most injuries during the study period (Table 3). Most reported injuries were to the knee 473
 (16%), hip/groin 347 (11%), and ankle 316 (10%) (Table 4). The majority of injuries occurred
 95 na
 secondary to player contact 2151 (71%). There were 343 (11%) undisclosed injuries identified.

 96
 ur
 97 Discussion
 Jo
 98 The most important finding of this study is that the injury rate during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-
 99 2021 NFL season was significantly higher than the injury rates during weeks 1-4 of the 2016-
100 2017, 2018-2019, and 2019-2020 NFL preseason and regular season. The findings of our study
101 confirmed our hypothesis that players were at a higher risk of injury during the early 2020-2021
102 regular season following cancellation of preseason games due to Covid 19. Our findings
103 highlight the importance of NFL training camp in preparing NFL athletes for the rigors of the
104 NFL regular season and its influence on injury prevention.

105 Similar to the findings of Feeley et al.14 and Elliott et al.15 we observed more injuries occurred
106 during the first two weeks of the NFL preseason 777 (60%) when compared with the second two
 107 weeks 515 (40%). This trend was noted to continue, less dramatically, during the 2020-2021
108 regular season in that 300 (52%) injuries occurred during the first two weeks while 282 (48%)
109 occurred during the second two weeks. The results of our study suggest that in the absence of an
110 NFL preseason injuries are more frequent during the early regular season, similar to the injury
111 trend noted by Feeley et al.14 during training camp. However, given the unprecedented nature of
112 the Covid-19 pandemic and its effect on the 2020-2021 NFL season, this finding should be
113 interpreted with this limitation in mind.

114 We speculate that similar factors as the ones proposed to account for the increased injury rate
115 noted in the early NFL preseason also contributed to the increased injury rate noted in NFL
116
of
 players during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular season. These factors include the relative
117 ro
 deconditioning and muscle weakness that occurs during the offseason,16,17 as well as fatigue,
118
119
-p
 which suggests that fatigued muscles are more vulnerable to injury.18,19 It is likely that the
 deconditioning of players during the early 2020 NFL regular season was similar to past NFL
120
re
 preseasons; however, during the 2020 season players were asked to play more time and at a
121
122
lP
 higher level than they would typically be expected to play during the early preseason,
 specifically starters. Thus, increased time and intensity of play in the context of baseline
123 na
 deconditioning likely explains why the injury rate during the early 2020 NFL season was higher
124
125
ur
 than the injury rate in past NFL preseasons. Our findings contribute to growing body of evidence
 that fatigue and deconditioning may place athletes at a higher risk for injury.

126
 Jo
 Saw et al. in their systematic review of subjective measures used to monitor an athletes response
127 to training noted subjective measures including mood disturbance, perceived stress and recovery,
128 and symptoms of stress, to be highly sensitive to an athlete’s well-being in response to acute and
129 chronic exercise loads.20 In light of these findings the NFL may consider implementing athlete
130 self-reported questionnaires in order to monitor athlete’s level of exhaustion. Benefits of
131 monitoring fatigue and athlete well-being include revealing the need for recovery in order to
132 prevent injury, guiding training and competition scheduling, and understanding changes in
133 athletic performance related to fatigue.2,21 To our knowledge, no such measures have been
134 practiced in attempt to reduce injury risk in professional football. Future investigations may be
135 useful in evaluation of these subjective measurement techniques and their efficacy in injury
136 reduction in the NFL.
 137 Limitations

138 This study, as well as other similar publications utilizing the well-established multistep protocol
139 to identify injuries in professional athletes through review of public records, is associated with
140 several limitations. This is a database study, and incomplete data entry and inaccurate reporting
141 of injuries could confound the season-to-season injury differences. Details regarding injury
142 diagnosis and management, including injury severity, exact pathology, imaging reports, and
143 exact medical clearance were not available for all players. Because injured players were
144 identified using public records, the possibility of reporting errors, and omissions exist. We did
145 not assess the rate of injuries over the entire season to see if the injury rates normalized as the
146
of
 season went on. Our study also lacks objective measures of deconditioning to correlate with
147 ro
 injury rates during COVID-19. Finally, there remains the possibility of selection bias in the
148
149
-p
 injured group in which only “newsworthy” players injured were reported on. We attempted to
 minimize this bias by corroborating reported injuries with two additional resources, but the data
150 is limited by what is publicly available.
re
151 Conclusions
lP
152
na
 The rate of injury in NFL players during weeks 1-4 of the 2020-2021 regular seasons was
153 ur
 significantly higher than three recent past NFL preseasons and regular seasons.

 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, The Influence of Cuff Width, Sex, and Race on Arterial Occlusion: Implications for Blood Flow Restriction Research, matches the filename (punctuation and spacing only differ).",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A laboratory study of 249 young adults aged 18 to 34 (102 men, 147 women) who had arterial occlusion pressure measured in the standing position with 5, 10 and 12 cm cuffs. Mean occlusion pressure fell as cuff width increased (145, 123 and 120 mmHg), and arm circumference and resting systolic pressure explained the most variance. Regression equations were derived and cross-validated, and men and non-Hispanic Black participants had higher pressures, with the sex difference small and the race comparison based on 59 Black and 173 White participants.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample was not athletes, and the study did not measure blood flow volume, exercise or training outcomes, so the equations are estimates for healthy young adults at rest. The racial comparison was analyzed retrospectively and limited to Black and White participants because of sample size.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the prediction equations as a validated way to set training pressure for athletes, but they were built and tested on non-athlete adults at rest and only for three cuff widths.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2016,
  "citation": "Jessee MB, Buckner SL, Dankel SJ, Counts BR, Abe T, Loenneke JP. The Influence of Cuff Width, Sex, and Race on Arterial Occlusion: Implications for Blood Flow Restriction Research. Sports Medicine. 2016.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-016-0473-5",
  "abstract": "The study examined upper arm arterial occlusion pressure (AOP) across three cuff widths (5, 10 and 12 cm) in 249 participants, and how individual characteristics, sex and race affect it. AOP was highest for the 5 cm cuff, and arm circumference and resting systolic pressure explained the most variance for each cuff. Men required greater pressures, and non-Hispanic Blacks required greater pressures than Whites after controlling for sex. Regression equations were created for each cuff width.",
  "tldr": "Wider blood flow restriction cuffs need less pressure to stop arterial flow, and arm circumference and resting systolic pressure explain most of the individual variation. Report the cuff width and set restriction relative to each person's occlusion pressure; the equations were built on healthy adults, not athletes.",
  "methods": "Participants had arm length, arm circumference and resting brachial blood pressure measured, then AOP was found in the standing position for each cuff with a Doppler probe at the radial artery, with 5 minutes of rest between cuffs applied in counterbalanced order. Repeated measures ANOVA compared cuff widths, hierarchical regression identified predictors, and a random 66% split was used to build and cross-validate equations.",
  "findings": "AOP differed by cuff width (p<0.001), with 145 mmHg for the 5 cm cuff, 123 mmHg for 10 cm and 120 mmHg for 12 cm. The full model (arm circumference, systolic and diastolic pressure, arm length and sex) explained 56 to 65% of the variance. Men had higher AOP than women at each width, with small effects (d 0.33 to 0.46). Non-Hispanic Blacks (n=59) had higher AOP than Whites (n=173) at each width (for example 154 vs 142 mmHg at 5 cm), with d of 0.66 to 0.76, which the authors describe as relatively small for prescribing BFR.",
  "limitations": "Participants were healthy adults aged 18 to 34, not athletes, and AOP was measured at rest in standing, not during exercise. Blood flow volume was not measured, only presence or absence of radial pulse. The racial comparison was a retrospective analysis limited to Black and White participants because of sample size.",
  "practicalImplications": "Because cuff width changes the pressure needed to occlude flow, training studies and programs should report the cuff width used and set pressure relative to each person's occlusion pressure. The authors suggest the equations can estimate occlusion pressure for three common cuff widths, but they were derived for healthy non-athletes and should be checked before use with athletes.",
  "athleteDev": "Cuff width changes the pressure needed to restrict arterial flow, so blood flow restriction training prescriptions for athletes should name the cuff and set pressure relative to the individual. {
 "id":"Q11",
 "sourceFile":"The influence of exercise-induced fatigue on inter-limb asymmetries - A systematic review.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The title in the text, The Influence of Exercise-Induced Fatigue on Inter-Limb Asymmetries: a Systematic Review, matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport","Soccer","Endurance Sport","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified","Healthy Athletes","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A systematic review of 13 studies (252 healthy participants: 173 men and 79 women) that measured inter-limb asymmetry before and after, or during, an exercise loading protocol. The authors report that the results depend on the loading protocol, the task and the measured parameter, with significant changes in some studies and none in others. They conclude that no explicit conclusion can be drawn about whether exercise-induced fatigue changes asymmetry, and study quality scores ranged from 14 to 17 of 18.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The 13 studies are small and heterogeneous in loads, tests and asymmetry equations, so no meta-analysis was possible. Injury outcomes were not measured, the review includes no upper-limb studies, and several included studies did not report effect sizes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this review as showing that fatigue causes inter-limb asymmetry and raises injury risk, but the authors say the evidence is too inconsistent to draw that conclusion.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Heil J, Loffing F, Büsch D. The Influence of Exercise-Induced Fatigue on Inter-Limb Asymmetries: a Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2020;6:39.",
   "doi":"10.1186/s40798-020-00270-x",
   "abstract":"The review asked how exercise-induced fatigue affects inter-limb asymmetries in healthy people. Thirteen studies were included, using running, jumping, squatting, soccer, rowing and race walking as loads, and the results depended on the load, the task and the parameter measured. The authors could not draw a clear conclusion and call for more systematic research, including sport-specific tasks and tests before, after and during loading.",
   "tldr":"Fatigue-related changes in limb asymmetry were inconsistent across 13 small studies, so the review cannot say whether fatigue raises the asymmetry that is linked to non-contact injury. Test asymmetry with sport-specific tasks before and after training, and do not rely on fixed asymmetry cut-offs.",
   "methods":"A PRISMA-guided search of Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, SURF and SPONET in January 2020 identified studies of healthy people that calculated inter-limb asymmetry before and after, or during, a loading protocol. Study quality was rated with a 9-item, 18-point scale adapted from Bishop et al., and effect sizes were calculated post hoc where missing.",
   "findings":"Thirteen studies (252 participants) were included. Results varied: for example, Bishop et al. found a large effect on jump height asymmetry during repeated sprints, but only between the last two sets and baseline, Bromley et al. found large effects of a soccer match on some SLCMJ measures, and most other comparisons were small or non-significant. The authors state that no explicit conclusion can be drawn about the effect of exercise-induced fatigue on asymmetries.",
   "limitations":"Protocols, tasks, asymmetry equations and outcomes differed too much for pooling, and many studies gave incomplete results or no effect sizes. Most included studies had small samples (about 10 to 40), two studies included athletes with a past ACL rupture, and none included upper limbs or measured injury outcomes.",
   "practicalImplications":"Choose asymmetry tests that reflect the sport's demands, such as single-leg countermovement jumps, and test before and after a session to see whether asymmetry changes in your own athletes. The authors recommend individual analysis, a control group and longitudinal data, and they state that group-level thresholds do not show who is at higher injury risk.",
   "athleteDev":"Use sport-specific asymmetry tests before and after loading to track changes within each athlete, since the review cannot say which tasks or protocols will show fatigue-related asymmetry. Report the asymmetry equation used so results can be compared across sessions.",
   "rtp":"The review does not support using fatigue-related asymmetry changes to decide return to play. The authors note that the common 10 to 15 percent asymmetry thresholds used for return-to-play decisions have been criticized as arbitrary, and that group means do not show an individual's injury risk."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":["paper.rtp: 'authors note the 10 to 15 percent criteria are arbitrary' -> the thresholds 'have been criticized as arbitrary' (text: 'these limits are criticized for being arbitrary and needing better empirical justification [19]')"],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "The influence of limb dominance on performance-based outcomes after ACL reconstruction.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, The Influence of Limb Dominance on Performance-Based Outcomes After ACL Reconstruction, matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A cross-sectional study of 279 patients (49.1% female, mean age 20.8 years) tested about 7.7 months after ACL reconstruction, comparing dominant-limb and nondominant-limb surgery, with dominance defined by the preferred kicking leg. Isometric knee extension limb symmetry index (LSI) was higher for dominant-limb surgery (73.7 vs 66.5%, P<0.001, d=0.42), and 18.7% vs 6.2% passed the 90% cut-off. Raw strength and most balance and hop measures did not differ, with small significant differences in 6-meter hop and COP distance LSI and in contralateral triple-hop distance.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The study is cross-sectional, so it cannot show that limb dominance causes differences or predicts reinjury. Athletic status was not reported, rehabilitation was not standardized or monitored, balance data are missing for some patients, and most significant differences were small.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as showing that limb dominance should change return-to-activity decisions, but the significant findings are small and isolated, and the study does not measure reinjury or return-to-sport outcomes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Hodges J, Bruce Leicht AS, Thompson XD, Werner BC, Diduch DR, Brockmeier SF, et al. The Influence of Limb Dominance on Performance-Based Outcomes After ACL Reconstruction. Sports Health. 2025.",
  "doi": "10.1177/19417381251343089",
  "abstract": "In 279 patients tested about 7.7 months after ACL reconstruction, limb dominance was associated with the pass status of isometric knee extension LSI, with dominant-limb surgery achieving more symmetric knee extension torque and higher pass rates. No other strength, balance or hop LSI pass status was associated with limb dominance. Raw strength and balance measures did not differ, and small differences were found in the 6-meter hop, COP distance and contralateral triple hop.",
  "tldr": "After ACL reconstruction, surgery on the dominant leg went with more symmetric isometric knee extension strength, but limb dominance did not change most other strength, balance or hop results. Consider limb dominance when reading knee extension LSI, but do not treat it as a reason to change standard criteria.",
  "methods": "Observational cross-sectional study at a university laboratory of patients 5.5 to 12 months after primary, unilateral ACL reconstruction. Patients completed isokinetic and isometric knee strength, COP balance, and single-leg hop, triple hop and 6-meter hop tests, and LSI was classified as pass at 90% or more. Limb dominance was the preferred kicking leg, and comparisons used chi-square and independent t tests.",
  "findings": "Isometric knee extension LSI pass status was associated with limb dominance (chi-square 10.09, P=0.001), with 25 of 134 dominant-limb cases and 9 of 145 nondominant-limb cases passing. Isometric knee extension LSI was higher for dominant-limb surgery (73.71 vs 66.50%, P<0.001, d=0.42). COP distance LSI (P=0.03, d=0.40, more symmetric with nondominant-limb surgery) and 6-meter hop LSI (P=0.02, d=0.25) also differed, and contralateral triple-hop distance was greater in the nondominant-limb group (P=0.03, d=0.23).",
  "limitations": "The sample was mostly older adolescents and young adults and was not described by athletic status. Some tests were incomplete, balance data were added later, rehabilitation compliance was not controlled, and limb dominance was defined by kicking leg, which the authors note is subjective. The design cannot show cause, and most significant differences had small effect sizes with LSI values near 100%.",
  "practicalImplications": "When a return-to-activity decision relies on knee extension LSI, clinicians may consider whether the surgery was on the dominant leg, since more dominant-limb cases passed the 90% cut-off for isometric extension. The authors advise caution because the dominance definition is subjective and most other measures were unaffected, so limb dominance should complement standard LSI criteria rather than replace them.",
  "athleteDev": "Limb dominance changed isometric knee extension symmetry in these patients after ACL reconstruction, so knee extension strength targets may be read with the dominance side in mind. The sample was not described as athletes, and the study did not test training methods, so it does not show which program corrects these differences.",
  "rtp": "The study can inform how clinicians read LSI at return-to-activity testing, but it cannot show that limb dominance changes reinjury risk or the timing of clearance. The authors call for future work on reinjury and on tailored rehabilitation for dominance-specific asymmetries."
 },

 }
}

{
 "id":"Q13",
 "sourceFile":"The influence of movement tempo on acute neuromuscular, hormonal, and mechanical responses to resistance exercise - A mini review.pdf",
 "decision":"DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"The article's own DOI is not printed anywhere in the extracted text (no DOI string appears in the body, header or footer). Content is complete and readable.",
 "doiMissing":true,
 "identityCheck":"The title in the text, The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise-A Mini Review, matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A mini review of acute studies on movement tempo in isotonic resistance exercise, based on a keyword search of seven databases and inclusion of peer-reviewed studies in healthy adults. The included studies, which had 6 to 42 participants each and were mostly resistance-trained men, showed that slower tempos reduced the repetitions possible at a given load in several studies and lowered 1RM in the one study that tested it, while total time under tension generally rose with slower tempos. Lactate, testosterone, growth hormone and cortisol responses were inconsistent across studies.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The search and selection are described briefly, with no counts of records screened and no pooled analysis, so the conclusions are a narrative synthesis. The included studies are small and differ in load, tempo, exercise and outcome, and most designs cannot separate eccentric from concentric effects.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat slower tempo as a reliable driver of hormone and lactate responses, but the authors report that these findings conflict across studies, and the included samples were mostly resistance-trained or recreationally active adults rather than competitive athletes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Wilk M, Tufano JJ, Zajac A. The Influence of Movement Tempo on Acute Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Mechanical Responses to Resistance Exercise: A Mini Review. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020;34(8):2369-2383.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"The review describes how premeditated movement tempo affects resistance training variables. Slower tempos reduce the 1RM, the load that can be used, and the number of repetitions performed at a given load, while increasing total time under tension, which can influence acute cardiovascular and hormonal responses. The authors suggest testing maximal strength and repetitions at each tempo used, because programming tempo without this testing is closer to trial and error.",
   "tldr":"Slower lifting tempos lower the repetitions possible and the 1RM, and increase total time under tension, but hormone and lactate responses vary between studies. Test 1RM at each tempo you plan to use, and track total time under tension as part of training volume.",
   "methods":"A mini review searched Google Scholar, MEDLINE, ADONIS, ERIC, SPORTDiscus, EBSCOhost and PubMed with paired keyword terms on tempo, time under tension, volume and acute responses. Included studies were original peer-reviewed English-language research in healthy adults that used isotonic resistance exercise, with no sex restriction. The authors also set a tempo classification (volitional, explosive, fast, medium, slow and extremely slow) and summarized each study's tempo, load, sample and findings.",
   "findings":"Slower tempos were associated with fewer repetitions at a given load in several studies and with lower 1RM in one study (about 3.7% lower with a 4/0/2/0 than a 2/0/2/0 tempo). Total time under tension increased with slower tempos, for example 178.8 s for 6/0/4/0 versus 124.65 s for 2/0/2/0 over five sets. Blood lactate, testosterone, growth hormone and cortisol responses were inconsistent across studies, with some finding greater responses at slower tempos and others finding no difference.",
   "limitations":"The authors note that most included studies cannot separate the effects of eccentric and concentric duration, and that load, volume, rest and exercise often differ between tempo conditions. The review does not pool results, and the studies are small and mostly in men or resistance-trained participants. Several conclusions are described by the authors as speculative and in need of further research.",
   "practicalImplications":"Test 1RM at each tempo used, since slower tempos reduce the load and repetitions that can be lifted, and set training loads from that test. Track total time under tension as well as repetitions when judging volume. The authors suggest slower tempos for controlled, time-under-tension work and faster concentric movement for power, and note that tempo can vary between sessions, sets or exercises.",
   "athleteDev":"Tempo changes the load, repetitions and total time under tension, so programs that specify tempo should base loads on a 1RM tested at that tempo. The authors suggest slower tempos may suit youth or injured athletes, but they do not test this, and they state there is a lack of data confirming that slower tempo harms power output.",
   "rtp":"The review mentions injured athletes only as a suggestion that controlled tempos may help manage load, and it reports no rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes. It cannot show that tempo training speeds return to sport or lowers reinjury risk."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "evidenceSummary: 1RM reduction 'in several studies' -> in the one study that tested it (text: 'One study examined the effect of 2 tempos ... on the maximal 1RM load'; 'To date, there is no data regarding the differences in 1RM load between fast and slow')",
     "synthesisCaution: 'tempo effects have not been tested in athletes' -> included samples were mostly resistance-trained or recreationally active adults (Table 7 samples)",
     "paper.athleteDev: 'found no data on tempo effects on power output in athletes' -> 'there is a lack of data confirming the negative impact of slower movement tempo on power output'",
     "populations: Mixed / Unspecified -> Adult / Recreational (included studies were healthy adults, mostly resistance-trained men, not athlete samples)",
     "degradedReason: removed the reference-list remark; confirmed no DOI string anywhere in the text"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Study design kept as Systematic Review / Meta-analysis under the rule for reviews with a described search (databases, keywords, inclusion criteria), but the paper is labeled a Brief Review with no screening counts or quality appraisal; a reviewer may prefer Narrative Review. DOI should be confirmed externally to upgrade from DEGRADED.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, The Influence of Psychological Factors on the Incidence and Severity of Sports-Related Concussions: A Systematic Review, matches the filename.",

 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "American Football", "Soccer", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified", "Youth / Adolescent", "Collegiate", "Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A PRISMA systematic review, registered in PROSPERO, of 10 studies on preexisting psychological factors and sports-related concussion in athletes of all sports, with samples from 40 to 1,246 athletes, mostly male. The authors report that meanness, aggression and psychoticism were linked to more concussions in one study of male football players, and that baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms were linked to worse symptoms after concussion. {
 "id": "Q15",
 "sourceFile": "The injury mechanism of Achilles tendon rupture in professional athletes - A video analysis study.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, The Injury Mechanism of Achilles Tendon Rupture in Professional Athletes: A Video Analysis Study, matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Case Report / Case Series",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Basketball", "American Football", "Soccer", "Baseball / Softball", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes", "Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "A retrospective observational series of 42 Achilles tendon ruptures in professional athletes (41 men and 1 woman, mean age 28.4 years; 18 basketball, 14 American football, 5 soccer, 3 baseball and 2 rugby players), analyzed from publicly available videos. Of the ruptures, 83.3% were noncontact, the most frequent game activities were take-off or acceleration (40.5%) and stop or rotate (38.1%), and at rupture the ankle was dorsiflexed in 71.4% and the trunk flexed in 73.8%. Three reviewers showed high agreement (Fleiss kappa above 0.864 intraobserver and above 0.815 interobserver).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Videos were non-standardized, so joint angles were not measured and positions are qualitative. Cases came from public online sources that may be incomplete or inaccurate, the sample is small, and it is mostly basketball and men, with no comparison group of uninjured athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the posture at rupture as a cause that drills can prevent, but the study only describes positions in a series of public videos and does not show that any position or drill changes rupture risk.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Yüce A, Yerli M, Misir A. The Injury Mechanism of Achilles Tendon Rupture in Professional Athletes: A Video Analysis Study. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2024;114(3).",
  "doi": "10.7547/21-196",
  "abstract": "The study used video analysis to describe how Achilles tendon ruptures occur in professional athletes and what body posture is present at the time of injury. Of 42 analyzed injuries, most occurred during take-off or acceleration, or during stopping and turning. At rupture, the ankle was in dorsiflexion, the body was bent forward, and the knee and hip were in extension. The authors suggest the findings can guide neuromuscular, proprioceptive and balance training to prevent rupture.",
  "tldr": "In this series of 42 professional-athlete ruptures, most happened without contact during take-off, acceleration or stopping and turning, with the ankle dorsiflexed and the trunk flexed. These movements can guide prevention drills, but the sample is small and based on public videos.",
  "methods": "A retrospective observational study identified 114 Achilles ruptures in professional athletes from 1970 to 2020 through internet searches. Of 48 videos accessed, 42 with adequate quality were analyzed by three reviewers who had not previously done video analysis and who scored each video blindly for contact, game activity and body position. Agreement was assessed with Fleiss kappa, and joint angles were not measured because the videos were not standardized.",
  "findings": "Of the 42 athletes, 35 (83.3%) had noncontact injuries, and the most frequent game activities were take-off or acceleration (40.5%), stop or rotate (38.1%) and landing (16.7%). At rupture, the ankle was dorsiflexed in 71.4%, the trunk was flexed in 73.8%, and the hip and knee were extended in 61.9% and 54.8% of cases. Intraobserver agreement was above 0.864 and interobserver agreement above 0.815.",
  "limitations": "Videos came from different platforms with different angles and quality, so joint angles could not be measured and only qualitative positions were recorded. Injury data came from public records that may not be complete or accurate, and the sample is small, almost all male, and led by basketball players (18 of 42). The abstract and discussion give 38.5% for stop or turn, while Table 2 gives 38.1% (16 of 42).",
  "practicalImplications": "The common activities (take-off, acceleration, stopping and turning) and the posture at rupture (ankle dorsiflexed, trunk flexed, knee and hip extended) can guide which movements to include in neuromuscular, balance and proprioceptive training. The authors also suggest sport-specific conditioning and strengthening, but the study did not test whether these reduce rupture rates.",
  "athleteDev": "The take-off, acceleration and stop-and-turn positions can guide sport-specific neuromuscular and balance drills, particularly for basketball players, who were 18 of the 42 cases. The study does not measure performance outcomes or show that these drills prevent ruptures.",
  "rtp": "The study does not inform return to sport. It does not report rehabilitation methods, surgical treatment or return-to-play criteria, although it notes that many athletes fail to return to their previous level. Its findings may help choose movements for prevention work, but they cannot guide clearance decisions."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "VERIFIED",
  "changes": [],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}
